subject: analyzing density vs. counts with trapping web data

messages.author: e1ad8e4570c0b9e5
messages.subject: analyzing density vs. counts with trapping web data
parts:
I have small mammal trapping web data from a designed experiment with 12=20
stands divided into control stands (3), and 3 fuel-reduction treatments,=20
each with 2-4 replicates. Each stand had one trapping web. I analyzed 2=20
species with good data: deer mice and yellow-pine chipmunks. Captures in=20
each of the 4 treatment ?strata? were insufficient for estimating separate =

detection functions, so I estimated a global detection function for each=20
species to estimate density in each treatment unit.=20

Each species has about 100 total detections, but the density estimate for =

deer mice was 15/ha whereas for chipmunks was 40/ha. I assume this is=20
because the detection functions differ, hence the density estimates=20
differ. Reviewers suspect a fatal flaw here, and suggest I simply use=20
the counts of individuals for each web in ANOVA, especially since I used a =

global detection function. Two questions:

Could you comment on the disparity between the density estimates between=20
the species given similar number of captures, i.e. am I correct in my=20
interpretation?=20

Is it correct to use the simple count data from the webs vs. the Distance=20
estimates? My guess is no.

I did an ANOVA of the density estimates, but understand there is the=20
covariance issue with the global detection function. I will investigate=20
Buckland?s methods for designed experiments, if that is your=20
recommendation and you do not recommend ANOVA of simple counts. Thanks.

messages.author: d718c6bb1db28db2
messages.subject: Re: analyzing density vs. counts with trapping web data
parts:
John, I would have thought that the disparity in density estimates was
proof, if any was needed, that you can't simply do an ANOVA on counts.
There clearly is a difference in trappability, so counts across species
are not comparable. There are other problems with trapping webs (e.g.
you must assume animals at the centre are certain to be trapped; it's
fairly critical to get the trap spacing right relative to home range
size; and they're very labour-intensive if you are to have reasonable
replication). We've been working on an alternative - trapping point
transects - for that reason. These do not assume certain detection at
the point, and require far fewer traps to be set. See J Appl Ecol 43,
377-384 (2006). The method works well if there isn't a strong response
to trapping. A research student of ours, Joanne Potts, has been
developing the method for use on woodrats.

Yes, the methods we used for analysis of designed experiments in
distance sampling (JABES 14, 432-442, 2009) should work OK. Cornelia
Oedekoven, a research student of ours, is also working on an integrated
approach, which we hope might be better than this 2-stage approach, but
we're not quite there yet.

Steve Buckland
